standard.title: Chemical Equations and Conservation of Mass
standard.description: model the rearrangement of atoms in chemical reactions using a range of representations, including word and simple balanced chemical equations, and use these to demonstrate the law of conservation of mass
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can compare physical and chemical changes and identify indicators of energy change in chemical reactions (AC9S8U07). They can classify matter as elements, compounds and mixtures and use chemical symbols and formulas (AC9S8U06). They can compare reversible and irreversible changes (AC9S6U04). They have not yet modelled atom rearrangement as the mechanism of chemical change, written balanced symbolic equations, or applied conservation of mass as a quantitative principle to chemical reactions.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students model chemical reactions as atom rearrangement using word equations, molecular models and balanced symbolic equations, and use conservation of mass — demonstrated through atom counting — to explain why equations must be balanced.

nodes.label: Reactants and products — identifying what changes in a chemical reaction
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify reactants and products in a chemical reaction and describe the change in terms of new substances being formed.
nodes.minimum_width: Students correctly identify reactants and products in a named reaction and state that new substances with different properties are formed.
nodes.typical_width: Students identify reactants and products in multiple reaction types; connect to prior physical vs chemical change knowledge from AC9S8U07 — new substances with different properties are the defining feature; explain that chemical change involves bond breaking and forming; describe observable evidence (colour change, gas production, precipitate, energy change) as indicators of product formation.
wider: Investigate why most elements are not found in their elemental state — what does their chemical reactivity tell us about the products formed in natural reactions?
Examine a combustion reaction in terms of reactants and products — identify all products, including water vapour, not just CO₂

response_modes.reason: Students have prior knowledge of chemical change indicators but not the reactant-product framing as a formal input-output model. Establishing this framing — reactants consumed, products formed — is the conceptual orientation for the atom rearrangement model in N2.

success_criteria: Identifies reactants and products in a named chemical reaction
Explains that chemical reactions produce new substances with different properties
Connects reactant-product change to prior indicators of chemical change (AC9S8U07)

nodes.label: Atom rearrangement — chemical reactions as atomic-level redistribution
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can model a chemical reaction as the rearrangement of atoms using molecular models or diagrams, showing that atoms are neither created nor destroyed.
nodes.minimum_width: Students use a molecular model or diagram to represent a simple reaction (e.g. hydrogen + oxygen → water) showing the same atoms before and after.
nodes.typical_width: Students model multiple reactions using molecular models, structural diagrams, or ball-and-stick representations; count atoms on each side to verify they match; explain that bonds between atoms break and reform to produce new arrangements; explain that the type and number of atoms is unchanged — only their arrangement changes; connect this to why mass is conserved.
wider: Investigate a reaction in a closed system (sealed container) and demonstrate conservation of mass by weighing before and after — relate the result to the atom rearrangement model
Use molecular modelling software to build reactant and product structures for a named reaction and confirm atom count matches
nodes.hinge_reason: Atom rearrangement is the mechanistic foundation of the conservation of mass principle and the conceptual basis for why equations must be balanced. Students who understand chemical change only at the observable level — new substance formed — cannot understand why balancing an equation is a meaningful scientific constraint rather than an arbitrary rule.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat balancing equations as a procedural task without understanding why it is required. Making atom rearrangement explicit — same atoms, new arrangement — is the conceptual move that makes conservation of mass a necessary consequence rather than an imposed rule.

success_criteria: Uses a molecular model or diagram to represent a simple reaction showing atoms before and after
Counts atoms on each side of a representation and confirms they match
Explains that atoms are rearranged — not created or destroyed — in chemical reactions

nodes.label: Word equations — naming reactants and products
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can write correct word equations for named chemical reactions, correctly identifying all reactants and products.
nodes.minimum_width: Students write a correct word equation for two named reactions.
nodes.typical_width: Students write word equations for combustion, neutralisation, and displacement reactions; include all products (including water in combustion); use correct arrow notation; explain the limitation of word equations — they name substances but do not show quantities or atom counts.
wider: Write word equations for First Nations Australians' chemical processes — e.g. reactions used to convert toxic plants into edible food — and identify reactants and products
Investigate green chemistry principles — examine a reaction used in industry and write the word equation, identifying any wasteful products and suggesting alternatives

response_modes.reason: Word equations require correct identification of all reactants and all products — a common error is omitting water or CO₂ in combustion. Structured practice with self-correction at the word equation level is the prerequisite for symbolic equation writing in N4.

success_criteria: Writes a correct word equation for at least two named reactions, including all products
Explains what word equations show and what they do not (no quantities, no atom counts)

nodes.label: Balanced symbolic equations — demonstrating conservation of mass
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can write and balance simple symbolic chemical equations and explain why balancing demonstrates the law of conservation of mass.
nodes.minimum_width: Students correctly balance a simple symbolic equation by adjusting coefficients (not subscripts) and verify by atom counting.
nodes.typical_width: Students balance symbolic equations for multiple reaction types; explain the rule that subscripts cannot be changed (they define the substance) while coefficients can; verify balance by atom counting on both sides; explain that a balanced equation is a model demonstrating conservation of mass; connect to the atom rearrangement model from N2 — balanced equations show the same atoms before and after.
wider: Write and balance symbolic equations for reactions used to obtain elements from their compounds (e.g. metal extraction) and explain what the balanced equation reveals about mass relationships
Apply conservation of mass quantitatively — given the mass of one reactant, predict the mass of product formed using the molar ratios in a balanced equation (introductory level)
nodes.hinge_reason: Balancing symbolic equations is the procedural and conceptual endpoint of the descriptor — it is the representation through which conservation of mass is demonstrated. Students who cannot balance equations cannot demonstrate conservation of mass, and persistent errors (changing subscripts, wrong atom counting) are systematic and require explicit correction before the law can be applied.

response_modes.reason: Balancing equations requires procedural precision across two constraints simultaneously: identifying which atoms need balancing, and adjusting only coefficients. Systematic errors — changing subscripts, miscounting polyatomic groups — are common and propagate into all subsequent chemistry work (AC9S10U07).

success_criteria: Balances a simple symbolic equation by adjusting coefficients (not subscripts)
Verifies a balanced equation by counting atoms of each element on both sides
Explains that a balanced equation demonstrates conservation of mass — same atoms, same total mass, on both sides

nodes.label: Conservation of mass — connecting representation to empirical evidence
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use balanced equations to explain the law of conservation of mass, and connect this to experimental evidence from reactions in closed and open systems.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain why a reaction in a closed system shows no change in total mass, and why an open system may appear to lose or gain mass.
nodes.typical_width: Students investigate or analyse data from closed system reactions to confirm mass conservation; explain apparent mass changes in open systems (gas escaping or being absorbed from air); use balanced equations to predict mass of products from known reactant masses; evaluate the claim that 'mass is conserved in chemical reactions' against experimental data.
wider: Investigate green chemistry principles — if mass is always conserved, why does green chemistry focus on waste? Reconcile atom economy with conservation of mass
Examine a reaction where mass appears to change in an open system and explain the discrepancy using conservation of mass — what left or entered the system?

response_modes.reason: This node integrates atom rearrangement (N2), word equations (N3) and balanced symbolic equations (N4) into an empirically grounded account of conservation of mass. Connecting the symbolic model to experimental data — particularly explaining open vs closed system discrepancies — is the descriptor's 'demonstrate the law of conservation of mass' demand.

success_criteria: Explains why total mass is conserved in a closed system chemical reaction
Explains apparent mass changes in open system reactions using conservation of mass
Uses a balanced equation to connect the symbolic representation to the empirical mass conservation result
